title: Why Staying Loyal to Your Job Keeps You Poorer
sources: Dramatized story: Dave, Kyle, Dave's boss, the salaries ($62,000, $71,000, $69,000), the posted range ($68,000-$74,000), the 2% raise and the mug are illustrative. Math: $71,000 - $62,000 = $9,000 a year; x 10 years = $90,000 (no raises or interest assumed). $69,000 - $62,000 = $7,000. Dave's $62,000 is close to the U.S. full-time median (BLS Usual Weekly Earnings, Q3 2025: $1,214 a week, about $63,000 a year).

Matthew Bidwell (Wharton), 'Paying More to Get Less: The Effects of External Hiring versus Internal Mobility', Administrative Science Quarterly 56(3), 2011; Knowledge at Wharton, March 28, 2012: personnel data from the U.S. investment banking division of a financial services firm, 2003-2009. External hires were paid about 18% to 20% more than workers promoted internally into similar jobs, got significantly lower performance evaluations for their first two years and had higher exit rates; they often had more education and experience.

Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, Wage Growth Tracker (data since 1997; via FRED series FRBATLWGT3MMAUMHWGJMJSW and ...JMJST, updated Oct 9, 2026), 3-month moving average of median 12-month wage growth: July 2022 job switchers 8.6% vs job stayers 6.0%; July 2025 switchers 4.0% vs stayers 4.1%; September 2026 switchers 4.7% vs stayers 3.4% (gap 1.3 points).

The Henry Ford (museum), 'Ford's Five-Dollar Day': labor turnover at Ford Motor Company was 370% in 1913; the company hired about 52,000 workers in a year to keep a workforce of 13,000-14,000; on January 5, 1914 Henry Ford and James Couzens announced the five-dollar day, roughly doubling pay; turnover then fell sharply.

Gold watch: widely repeated account (e.g. McTear's Auctioneers, 'The Gift of Gold') that Pepsi-Cola popularized the retirement gold watch in the 1940s with the line 'you gave us your time, now we are giving you ours'. Presented in the script as 'the story goes'.
WTW Salary Budget Planning Report (July 2026; survey March-May 2026): U.S. salary increase budgets averaged 3.5% in 2026, 3.4% projected for 2027. Callback: episode 32 (raises vs prices).

Google, November 2010: internal memo from CEO Eric Schmidt giving all roughly 23,000 employees a 10% raise from January 2011 (plus a $1,000 bonus), amid departures to Facebook; reported by Fortune and Business Insider (Nov 9-10, 2010).
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Job Openings and Labor Turnover, August 2026 (USDL-26-1547, Sept 29, 2026): hires rate 3.3%, quits rate 1.9%.

Colorado Equal Pay for Equal Work Act (SB 19-085), in force January 1, 2021: job postings must include the pay rate or range. Since then more than a dozen states (among them California, New York, Washington, Illinois, Minnesota, New Jersey, Massachusetts, Vermont, Hawaii, Maryland) plus Washington DC have passed pay-range disclosure laws; details and employer-size thresholds differ by state.
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics (bls.gov/oes): free wage estimates for about 830 occupations, by state and metro area.

Pew Research Center, 'When negotiating starting salaries, most U.S. women and men don't ask for higher pay' (April 5, 2023; survey Feb 2023): 60% of workers did not ask for higher pay the last time they were hired; among those who asked, 28% got what they asked for and 38% got more than first offered but less than they asked (66% got more), 35% got only the first offer.
Callbacks: episode 32 (raise), episode 59 (Dad's pension = the vending machine), episode 60 teaser (2% after five loyal years).

youtube.title: Why Staying Loyal to Your Job Keeps You Poorer
alt_titles: Why the New Hire Makes More Than You (For the Same Job)
Your Company Pays Strangers More Than You. Here's Why.
youtube.hook: The new hire at the next desk may be paid more than you for the same job. Why that happens, and how Dave got $7,000 more without quitting.
tags: new hire paid more than me
how to ask for a raise
youtube.pinned: How many years have you been at your current job? Drop the number below.

beats.text: This is me at my five year work anniversary. My boss gives me a gift bag. Inside there's a mug.
And a letter with my raise. Two percent.
Then I walk to the printer and see the offer letter for the new guy. Same job. Nine thousand dollars more than me.
And I'm the one training him.
By the end of this video you'll know why loyal people get paid less and the three moves I used to get seven thousand more without quitting.
But most people click away before that part. Which is exactly what your company is hoping for.
So let me back up. I've been at this job five years. I'm good at it. I know where the good stapler lives.
The new guy is Kyle. He started Monday. Same title. Same team. And his starting pay is seventy one thousand. Mine is sixty two.
And Kyle is nice. That's the worst part. I can't even hate him. He brought donuts on his first day.
Me showing Kyle where the coffee machine is.
Somewhere upstairs somebody looked at a real raise and said no. Then looked at a mug and said yes.
Nine thousand a year. Over ten loyal years that's ninety thousand dollars. For being loyal.
Be honest. You would have read that letter too. And then at midnight you'd type new hire paid more than me is this legal.
The internet answers in four seconds. Yes it's legal. And it's so common it has a name. Salary compression.
Here's what it means. The pay for new people climbs with the market. The pay for people already inside creeps up slowly. Until the new guy passes you.
Think of your salary like a price sticker with a date on it. My sticker says five years ago. Kyle's sticker says last Monday.
Nobody ever updates my sticker. Unless I ask. And I never ask. Because asking feels rude.
My salary sticker versus Kyle's.
And there's a scoreboard for this. The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta tracks people who stay at their job and people who switch.
In the summer of twenty twenty two the switchers were getting raises of almost nine percent. The stayers got six. And I got a mug.
My pay chart versus Kyle's pay chart.
So try this on yourself. Do you know what your company would pay a stranger to do your job today? Most people have no idea. I sure didn't.
And right by the elevator there's an old photo of a guy named Walt getting a gold watch for thirty years here. So when did staying stop paying?
Because companies really did pay people to stay. And the best story is Henry Ford.
In nineteen thirteen his assembly line was so boring that he had to hire fifty two thousand people in one year just to keep fourteen thousand jobs filled.
Ford's workers in nineteen thirteen.
So in nineteen fourteen Ford doubled the pay to five dollars a day. And the quitting pretty much stopped.
He wasn't being sweet. He did the math. Losing people cost him more than paying them.
For decades that was the deal. You stayed thirty years. You got a pension. And on your last day they handed you a gold watch.
My dad's whole generation had this deal. Stay loyal and the company takes care of you. He still gets a check every month from a job he left twenty years ago.
Me looking at my mug. It does not tell time.
Then somewhere along the way the deal flipped. And to show you how far it flipped I need you to guess something.

A Wharton professor looked at six years of pay records at one big company. Outside hires versus insiders promoted into the same kind of job. How much more did the outsiders get? Put your guess in the comments.
So the next morning I walk into my boss's office and ask her straight. Why does Kyle make more than me?
And my boss actually likes me. So she sighs and tells me the truth. Dave. It's two different pots of money.
Pot one is the raise pot for everyone already working here. This year a typical company filled it with about three and a half percent.
Three and a half percent. That's barely more than prices went up. So my raise isn't a raise. It's a refund for inflation.
Pot two is the hiring pot. And it works differently. A stranger won't sign unless you pay what the job is worth today.
So the hiring pot follows the market. The raise pot follows the budget. And every year they drift a little further apart.
The company deciding where the money goes.
It's like a family that brings home a new puppy and buys it steak. And the old dog who guarded the house for five years gets the same dry kibble.
Nobody thinks the old dog is going anywhere. That's the whole reason he gets kibble.
And I say wait. Am I the old dog? Yes Dave. I'm the old dog.
The company walking with me and staring at Kyle.
Now back to your guess. In that study the outsiders got paid about eighteen to twenty percent more.
And here's the part that should make you a little angry. Who got better reviews for the first two years? The insiders. The company paid more to get less.
They had their best people sitting right there. Cheaper and better. And they paid more for strangers anyway.
The people upstairs making that decision.
To be fair the outsiders often had more experience on paper. And it costs extra to pull someone out of a safe job.
So nobody upstairs is twirling a mustache. The villain is a spreadsheet with two pots. And one quiet bet that you won't leave.

card.t: A bet that you won't leave.

beats.text: So I test it on myself. How many times in five years did I seriously look for another job? Zero.
You're probably the same. Because switching is scary. You'd be the new guy who doesn't know where they keep the good coffee.
At my job the coffee is terrible but at least I know exactly where it is.
I always thought if I kept my head down and worked hard somebody upstairs would notice. Nope. From upstairs a worker who never asks looks exactly like a happy one.
Think about your phone company. Your internet company. Your insurance. The new customer always gets the deal. The loyal one gets the bill. Your job is the same game.
Me for five years at my desk.
Now watch what happens when a company stops feeling sure. In twenty ten Google engineers started leaving for a hot young company called Facebook.
So the boss sent a memo giving every single employee a ten percent raise. All at once.
Ten percent. For everyone. Overnight. Because they were scared of losing people.
The money was there the whole time. It just took fear to open the pot.
Me finding out the money was there the whole time.
So I make the obvious decision. If leaving is the only language they understand then fine. I quit.
That night I write the most dramatic resignation letter of my life. It has the word furthermore in it twice.
I read it out loud to my cat. She left the room. Even my cat doesn't want to hear about my job.
But before I hit send I check that scoreboard again. And the bonus for switching comes and goes. Right now companies are hiring slowly. Fewer doors to walk through.
And jumping has its own price. You're the newest name on the list if layoffs come. And you can leave behind retirement money that isn't fully yours yet.
And the new job might be worse. Worse boss. Worse commute. Worse coffee. Nobody tells you that part on job sites.
Me choosing between staying and leaving.
I drop my head on the desk and knock the mug on the floor. The handle snaps off. Even the mug is leaving.
And that's when I notice there was a third door. And it was inside my own building the whole time.
Quick reminder this is education and not advice. But here's what I did. Three moves.
Move one. Find out what your job is worth today. And the easiest place to look was my own company's careers page.
Because starting with Colorado in twenty twenty one more than a dozen states now make employers put the pay range right in the job ad.
And there it was. My exact job. Posted by my own company. Sixty eight to seventy four thousand. Hi. I'd like to apply for my own job please.
Me applying for my own job.
If your state doesn't do that yet the government publishes what hundreds of jobs pay in your city. For free.
Ten minutes of searching. That's all it took to find out I was nine thousand dollars behind.
Move two. Change the question. Ask for a raise and you get sent to pot one. The tiny pot. So I asked for a market adjustment. Which is office language for please update my sticker.
Same money. Fancier name. And somehow the office loves it.
Move three. Make it easy to say yes. I wrote one page. Three things I did this year that saved the company money. And one number at the bottom. Seventy one thousand.
Not a speech. Not a threat. Just facts on one page. Bosses love pages. They can forward a page upstairs.
Does asking even work? Most workers never ask for more pay when they're hired. But of the ones who did ask about two out of three got more money.
People who never ask versus people who ask.
So Thursday morning I glue the handle back on my mug for luck and knock on her door. I don't threaten to quit. I don't mention Kyle. I just slide the page across the desk.
I like it here and I want to stay. But the market rate for my job is seventy one thousand and I'd like to talk about closing that gap.
She reads it twice. Then she says the four most annoying words in business. Let me check upstairs.
Two very long weeks. A lot of nervous coffee out of a glued together mug.
Every time my boss walked past my desk I pretended to type very important things.
Then the email arrives. They can't do seventy one. But they can do sixty nine thousand starting next month.
That's seven thousand more a year. And I never quit. I never had to learn where a new building keeps the good coffee.
My pay chart finally gets its own little rocket.
It doesn't always go like that. Sometimes the answer is no. But even then you know exactly what you're worth. And the other doors are still there.
Because loyalty is a great thing to give a company. It's just a terrible thing to give away for free.

card.t: Don't give loyalty away for free.

beats.text: And Kyle is doing great. In about five years somebody should probably warn him about the mug.
So here's the deal. Your company isn't evil. It's just betting you won't ask. Go win the bet.
Next time I celebrate by buying something for nine ninety nine. My brain files it under nine dollars. And stores have known that trick forever.
Subscribe. It's free. And unlike your boss we'll actually notice that you stayed.
